I run audit kickoffs for a living, and the first ten minutes always tell me how the next six weeks will go. I ask one simple question: walk me through your close. Some people give me a list. We do the accruals, then the reconciliations, then the reporting. That is fine, but it leaves me with twenty follow-up questions. The people I remember answer in three or four long sentences, and every sentence carries an extra piece of context in the middle. Our close, which covers four entities, takes five business days. The reconciliations, which the shared service center prepares, come to me on day three. When I hear that, I know who does what, how big it is, and where the risk sits. I have not had to ask a single follow-up question, and the meeting finishes early.

When I joined the group as controller for Canada, I had calls with about thirty people in my first two weeks. Most of them introduced themselves with a job title and a team name, and by Friday I could not remember any of them. One person was different. She said: I am the accountant who looks after the Brazil close, which is the biggest entity in the region, and I am the person the auditors call when a number needs explaining. That is one sentence, and it told me her scope, her ownership and when to call her. I called her the next month, because I knew exactly what she was accountable for. A title tells me where you sit. The extra clause tells me why I should remember you.
